channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: After talks with President Trump at the White House on 24 September, President Xi Jinping said China and the US had reached a "new joint arrangement" on trade; no details were given.
item.description:
The South China Morning Post calls the arrangement ill-defined and reports that Trump suggested the two sides had made progress on a Board of Trade mechanism to reduce tariffs on non-strategic products in equal measure. Handelsblatt reports that Xi spoke of "many new agreements" without giving details. The Chinatimes reports that a US–China trade committee is discussing market access and tariffs for non-sensitive goods such as medical equipment, energy, consumer goods and agricultural products, while dual-use technologies, artificial intelligence and advanced chips remain subject to export controls. According to the Commercial Times and the Chinatimes, negotiations on rare-earth supply, agricultural purchases and tariffs on non-sensitive goods are still pending. The trade truce had already been extended before the talks, from 10 November to 10 January 2027, which US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said gives the two sides more time on the economic front. The reporting does not say which products or tariff lines the arrangement covers, when it would take effect, or whether it is written down.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The summit produced a statement of intent rather than a schedule: the only dated element in the reporting is the truce extension to 10 January 2027. The Board of Trade mechanism, as Trump described it, is aimed at reducing tariffs on non-strategic goods in equal measure, which, on a general reading, is the category where most industrial intermediates and consumer products sit, while technology-related goods stay under export controls. Rare-earth supply, which on a general reading reaches electronics and automotive supply chains, is among the open points. Points that may be worth considering include which US–China product flows would fall into a "non-strategic" category, and what the lack of published terms means for planning that assumes the current tariff levels after 10 January 2027.

South China Morning Post | CNA | Handelsblatt | Chinatimes | Commercial Times | MarketScreener

item.title: The German government has called on the EU to open the planned "Made with Europe" rules in the Industrial Accelerator Act to countries outside the bloc, according to a position paper obtained by Euronews, while France emphasises the 27 member states.
item.description:
The draft law would restrict public procurement — government contracts for goods such as steel, batteries and electric vehicles — to products and companies meeting minimum EU production requirements. The Commission wants state subsidies and contracts in critical sectors to be linked to production in Europe. German Economy Minister Katherina Reiche again argued in Brussels for including trading partners, while French Industry Minister Sébastien Martin emphasised the EU-27. According to the Süddeutsche Zeitung, the Commission's plans cover cars, heat pumps and photovoltaic systems as well as important building materials such as cement and aluminium; the aim is to keep industrial production in Europe despite competition from countries such as China. The reporting does not say which partner countries Germany would include, what the minimum production requirements would be, or when the Council is expected to decide.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The German–French split is over the definition of "European" in procurement, which decides whether goods produced in partner countries count. For a supplier to the listed sectors — cars, heat pumps, photovoltaics, cement and aluminium — the practical question is whether the products its customers sell into public contracts would need a European production share, and, on a general reading, whether that requirement reaches into the materials those products contain. The reporting does not say whether minimum production requirements would extend to components or materials. Points that may be worth considering include which customer segments sell substantial volumes into public procurement, and whether production outside the EU in partner countries would count under the German approach.

Euronews | Süddeutsche Zeitung | Wallstreet:online

item.title: The International Federation of Robotics reports that 24,800 industrial robots were installed in Germany in 2025, 8% fewer than a year earlier, mainly because of weaker demand from manufacturing.
item.description:
Germany still accounts for 41% of installations in the EU and ranks fifth worldwide, behind South Korea, Japan, the US and China. The automotive industry remained the largest buyer in Germany with 5,800 new robots, 23% of the total, despite declining demand. In China, installations rose 20% to 354,000 units, 59% of global installations; the automotive industry there installed 78,900 units, up 38%, electrical and electronics 96,400, up 16%, and metal and machinery 78,700, up 44%. Wallstreet:online adds that three out of five systems installed worldwide are now Chinese, a record. The figures are for installations in 2025, so they describe installations last year, not this year. The reporting does not give 2026 data or break down German installations by industry beyond automotive.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Robot installations are an indicator of manufacturing investment, and the two countries moved in opposite directions: German installations fell 8% as manufacturing demand weakened, while Chinese installations rose 20%. On a general reading, automated assembly is where bonding and dispensing processes are specified alongside the robot cell, so installation data give a view of where new automated production lines are being built. The German automotive figure shows the sector remained the largest buyer despite declining demand. Points that may be worth considering include how much new automated capacity in the automotive customer base is being installed in China rather than Europe, and whether automated dispensing requirements differ between the two markets.

Handelsblatt | Wallstreet:online | Wallstreet:online | Xinhua

item.title: US new-home sales were 2% lower in August 2026 than a year earlier, at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 684,000, with the median price up 0.4% to USD 393,700, according to the Commerce Department.
item.description:
A separate count by the Associated General Contractors of America (AGC) shows construction employment rose in 235, or 66%, of 358 US metro areas between August 2025 and August 2026. Phoenix-Mesa-Chandler added the most jobs (6,800, or 4%), and Mobile, Alabama, had the largest percentage increase (11%). The largest loss was in Riverside-San Bernardino-Ontario, California (4,600 jobs, or 4%), and the steepest percentage decline in Fairbanks, Alaska (7%). The two measures cover different things: new-home sales are a residential demand figure, and construction employment covers all construction activity in each area. The reporting does not give the month-on-month change in new-home sales, the national change in construction employment, or the split between residential and non-residential jobs.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Read together, the figures describe a US construction market where residential sales are slightly below last year while construction employment is rising in most metro areas, which, on a general reading, points to activity being carried by segments other than new single-family sales; the reporting does not show which. A flat median price with lower sales does not indicate rising demand. The metro extremes — Phoenix and Mobile gaining, Riverside and Fairbanks losing — show a wide spread, though the reporting does not show a regional pattern. Points that may be worth considering include how US construction demand plans weight residential against non-residential work, and in which metro areas construction employment growth is concentrated.

Dünya | AGC

item.title: Germany's leading economic research institutes now expect GDP to grow 1.3% in 2026, up from 0.6% in their spring forecast, and 1.1% in 2027, up from 0.9%.
item.description:
The institutes presented their autumn report in Berlin. They name a boost in exports and the government's expansionary, debt-financed fiscal policy for infrastructure and defence as supports, with a continuing boom around artificial intelligence as possible additional impetus. They expect private consumption and housing construction to pick up next year. Oliver Holtemöller of the IWH warned that the recovery rests on a narrow foundation, because high energy prices and structural problems remain a burden; the Iran war and the sharp rise in energy prices had initially dampened the economy significantly. The institutes also say company capacities may increasingly reach their limits, and they forecast growth of only 0.4% for 2028. Separately, the ifo Institute's Timo Wollmershäuser told WirtschaftsWoche that the economy has been on the upswing since the end of 2025 and that Germany underestimated how much it benefited from the AI boom. The reporting does not give sector breakdowns or the energy-price assumptions behind the forecast.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The forecast is a forecast, not an outcome, and the IWH's Holtemöller describes the base as narrow: exports and public spending carry it, while the structural problems remain and growth falls back to 0.4% in 2028 on their numbers. The expected pick-up in housing construction next year is the part that reaches construction materials demand directly; the reporting does not give a figure for it. For planning, the profile — higher in 2026 and 2027, weak thereafter — may matter more than the headline number. Points that may be worth considering include whether German construction demand plans assume the pick-up in housing construction the institutes expect, and how exposed current German volumes are to infrastructure and defence spending rather than private demand.

Süddeutsche Zeitung | Wallstreet:online | WirtschaftsWoche

item.title: Sasol is investing EUR 60 million at its Brunsbüttel site in Germany to expand its capacity for catalyst carriers, according to a Sasol Germany item carried by Handelsblatt.
item.description:
The company says the expansion is expected to increase energy efficiency and reduce the CO2 footprint per tonne of catalyst carrier produced by up to 15%. In the same item, Antje Gerber, Executive Vice President of Sasol's international chemical business, says the chemical industry in Europe and Germany must produce more efficiently, drive innovation and focus more on high-quality specialty products to remain competitive. She names high energy and raw-material costs, international competition, stricter regulation and the transition to a climate-neutral economy as the pressures, and advanced materials, catalyst carriers, specialty surfactants and circular-economy and energy-transition solutions as the opportunities. It does not say how much capacity is added, when the expansion is completed, or how many jobs are involved.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

On a general reading, an investment in a German chemical site stands out against the cost pressures the item lists, and it follows the specialisation argument the item makes: a higher-value product line rather than base volume. The CO2 reduction is stated per tonne, which is an intensity measure, so it does not by itself say how total emissions at the site change as capacity grows. Specialty surfactants, one of the named opportunity areas, are, on a general reading, formulation ingredients in several downstream industries. Points that may be worth considering include whether other European producers are following the same specialisation route, and how that changes the availability of specialty raw materials from European sites.

Handelsblatt (press portal)

item.title: Austria, Czechia, Hungary, Slovakia and Poland are pushing for changes to the EU carbon market to give European industry more time and flexibility to cut emissions, according to a document seen by Euronews.
item.description:
The five countries argue that companies face very high costs to decarbonise factories while competing with producers outside Europe that do not pay the same carbon price. Austrian Industry and Energy Minister Wolfgang Hattmannsdorfer called for something like an "export discount", saying companies have a large problem when they start doing business outside the EU. The document is a position of five member states, not a Commission proposal. The reporting does not say which changes to the emissions trading system the countries propose, whether other member states support them, how an export discount would work, or when the Commission is expected to respond.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The request addresses the carbon cost European industry carries and its competitiveness in export markets, where, as the five countries argue, the European carbon price is not matched. An export discount would, on a general reading, address the export side, which, also on a general reading, the EU's carbon border adjustment does not cover for goods leaving the EU. Five mainly Central European states are a minority of the Council, so the paper shows direction of pressure rather than likely outcome. Points that may be worth considering include how much of current production cost in European plants is linked to carbon prices, and which of the changes, if adopted, would affect upstream suppliers of chemical raw materials.

Euronews

item.title: Mercedes-Benz is seeking to save up to EUR 800 million in labour costs in Germany, according to insiders cited by WirtschaftsWoche, and its production head has warned that otherwise a German car plant and a powertrain-component plant would have to close.
item.description:
Head of Production Michael Schiebe made the warning at a works meeting in Sindelfingen, according to the report. The company is asking employees for unpaid additional hours, citing high German wage costs: the talks concern up to five more hours a week — 40 instead of 35 — at the same pay. Cutting or cancelling holiday and Christmas pay or other special payments is also described as conceivable. The head of the general works council, Ergun Lümali, is reported to have explored whether committee members would accept concessions, and to have floated two extra hours a week for a limited two years, but only if Mercedes invests, commits products and keeps jobs and sites in Germany. The reporting does not name the plants at risk, give a timetable for the talks, or say how the EUR 800 million figure is made up.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The figure and the closure warning are negotiating positions, not decisions, and the savings figure comes from insiders rather than the company. What the report does show is that the site footprint of a large German vehicle manufacturer is now explicitly tied to a labour-cost outcome, with a car plant and a powertrain plant named as the alternative to savings. For suppliers, a plant closure would move volume rather than necessarily remove it, and where it moves decides which supply relationships carry it, on a general reading. The idea reportedly floated by the works council head links concessions to investment and product commitments in Germany, which, on a general reading, is the part that would fix future volume at German sites. Points that may be worth considering include how much German automotive volume is linked to Mercedes powertrain and assembly sites, and how the outcome of these talks may shape similar negotiations at other German manufacturers.

WirtschaftsWoche

item.title: French carmaker Renault announced on 24 September a EUR 600 million investment in Spain by 2030 to produce five new models, two of them electric, at its plants in Valladolid and Palencia.
item.description:
The investment combines the group's own resources with national and regional public aid, according to Le Dauphiné Libéré. The announcement allocates new model production to Renault's two Spanish plants over the rest of the decade. The reporting does not say which models are involved, how the five are split between the two plants, what production volumes are planned, when each model starts, or how much of the EUR 600 million is public aid. It also does not say whether the new models replace existing production at those plants or add to it, so the effect on total output in Spain cannot be judged from the report.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

A model allocation is the moment at which material and supplier choices for a vehicle are made, so an investment of this kind points to new sourcing decisions for bonding, sealing and assembly materials at the two Spanish plants over the coming years, on a general reading. Two of the five models are electric, which, also on a general reading, brings battery and battery thermal-management applications that combustion models do not have. The public-aid component shows national and regional authorities are supporting the investment; the size of that support is not given. Points that may be worth considering include which of the five models are already in development with defined supplier lists, and how Spanish automotive volume compares with other European production locations in current plans.

Le Dauphiné Libéré

item.title: India's Food Safety and Standards Authority (FSSAI) said on 23 September that products high in sugar, salt or fat would carry red warning symbols even if only one of those ingredients exceeds the limits.
item.description:
Under the earlier plan, a warning would have been required only when two ingredients breached the thresholds. Activists and health experts had criticised that plan as too lenient, and the Supreme Court of India questioned the approach. The FSSAI now says the warning labels will be rolled out in a single phase. It will issue and finalise the labelling regulations in about four months, after which the industry will have one year to implement the stricter labelling. The report describes the change as a setback for an industry worth about USD 100 billion. The reporting does not give the thresholds for each ingredient, the design or size of the symbol, which product categories are covered, or an estimate of how many products would need new labels.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The decision widens the rule from products breaching two limits to products breaching any one, so, on a general reading, the number of packs that need a new front-of-pack design rises; the reporting gives no count. A one-phase rollout with a one-year implementation period after final rules means label and pack artwork changes would, on a general reading, fall into one window, which is where printed labels, packaging films and cartons — and the adhesive technologies used to apply and laminate them — are affected, on a general reading. On a general reading, recipe reformulation to stay below the limits is the other route companies may take. Points that may be worth considering include how much packaged-food label volume in India is linked to multinational food customers, and whether a concentrated relabelling period changes demand timing for label stock.

TuoiTreNews

item.title: The European Commission has warned the US against banning diesel exports, saying such a move would hurt both markets, while US business groups have asked President Trump to resist calls for a ban.
item.description:
Commission spokesperson Olof Gill said on 24 September that the EU is concerned about reports that the US is considering a ban and that high-level contacts with the US government are ongoing. The Guardian reports that Trump is said to be considering a 90-day ban to ease pump prices before the midterm elections, with US diesel at a record average of USD 6.52 a gallon. The White House has denied a 90-day ban, and Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the US would take a voluntary approach with the refining industry and announce a policy in the coming days. The Business Roundtable, the American Petroleum Institute and more than two dozen other groups wrote that a ban would reduce refinery output and raise prices of gasoline and jet fuel. La Tribune cites Argus Media's Josh Michalowski that the US supplied about half of European diesel imports in August, after Europe replaced some Russian volumes with US Gulf Coast flows; Russia suspended its own diesel exports in July. The reporting does not show that any restriction has been decided, and it does not say which measures the voluntary approach would include.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The new element is the size of the dependency: with about half of European diesel imports coming from the US in August, a full US ban would put at risk a supply source that, according to the Argus figure, provided about half of European diesel imports in August. The outcome is open — the White House denies a ban and points to voluntary measures, while the Commission and US business groups argue against one. For a manufacturer, the exposure runs through road freight for inbound materials and outbound distribution, and, on a general reading, through carrier fuel surcharges rather than directly. Points that may be worth considering include what share of logistics cost is linked to diesel indices in freight contracts, and how quickly a US policy announcement in the coming days would feed through to European surcharges.

The Guardian | Chinatimes | La Tribune | Handelsblatt | Asharq Al-Awsat | Hong Kong Economic Times

item.title: A member survey by the Chemical Industry Federation of Finland finds that 78% of the sector's chief executives expect the conflict in the Strait of Hormuz to affect their company negatively, and 86% if the crisis continues into 2027.
item.description:
The federation says the negative effects come mainly from higher transport and energy costs, which companies cannot pass directly on to the prices of their own products. At the same time, 28% of companies describe their situation as good or very good and 30% as poor or very poor, which the federation calls the best reading since 2022 — so the survey pairs the best situation reading since 2022 with a large majority expecting negative effects from the conflict. 55% of responding member companies report that the prices of production inputs they buy from Europe have risen, and a slightly larger share say the situation has reduced their exports to Central Europe more than it has increased them. Separately, Handelsblatt reports Brent crude for November delivery up 3.7% to USD 107 a barrel, with Iran's Mohsen Rezaei saying the Strait of Hormuz would not be reopened until Iran's conditions were met. The reporting does not give the number of respondents, the survey dates, or how large the cost increases are.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The survey measures expectations, not results, but it names the mechanism: cost increases in transport and energy that the respondents say they cannot pass on. That is a margin question before it is a volume question. For a chemical industry that is one step upstream of many formulators, it also indicates where price pressure on intermediate products may come from, since 55% report higher prices for inputs sourced in Europe. Finland is a small chemical market, and on a general reading the pattern may differ in larger producer countries, but, on a general reading, the survey is one of the few measured reads from an industry association on how the conflict reaches company level. Points that may be worth considering include how much of the current transport and energy cost increase has been passed on in supplier price lists, and whether a crisis continuing into 2027 is part of current planning assumptions.

Kemianteollisuus | Handelsblatt
